name: ArchitecturalSection
doc:
A bounded region of the dual-stack architecture with
a characteristic purpose, representational formalism,
persistence mechanism, and set of interfaces to
neighbouring sections.
20 sections identified across the architecture.
Name-based identity (kebab-case identifiers stored
in the name attribute);

name: CustomerSegment
doc:
A defined group of customers with shared needs,
behaviours, and willingness to pay. Each segment
has distinct needs and may require distinct value
propositions.

purposiveDescription.description: A group of people your service is designed for — people who share similar needs and reasons for choosing you. When you define your customer segments, the system uses them to connect your value propositions, pricing, and channels to the right audiences.

weightedRelationships.rationale: Each segment has one or more propositions designed for it. A change to the target segment requires reassessing the value promises made to it.
Offerings are what the segment actually receives. A change to the target audience requires reassessing what is offered to them.
Channels are how segments are reached. A change to the target segment may require reviewing acquisition and delivery channels, but the relationship is many-to-many.

purposiveDescription.description: The core promise your service makes to a particular group of customers — what they get from you and why they'd choose you over the alternatives. When you define a value proposition, the system holds it as the anchor that your activities, resources, and pricing all exist to deliver.

weightedRelationships.rationale: The offering is the concrete realisation of the proposition. A change to the value promise requires reassessing what is offered to deliver it.

Claims articulate how the proposition differs from alternatives. A change to the proposition may require reviewing its supporting claims, but a proposition can exist before claims are formalised.

userFacing.shortDescription: The entity upon which a service is performed — a person, animal, object, or organisation that receives the service.

purposiveDescription.description: The thing your service acts on — the dog being groomed, the patient receiving care, the garment being cleaned, the item being repaired. A service subject may have needs independent of whoever commissioned the service, and governance obligations may attach to the subject directly. When you identify your service subjects, the system tracks what is being served, in what condition, and with what independent requirements — separately from who is paying or making decisions.

weightedRelationships.rationale: What is offered depends directly on the nature of the subject. A different breed, clinical condition, or item type requires reassessing the offering.
Governance obligations attach to the subject independently of the customer. Duty of care is to the dog, the patient, the object in custody.
The subject's characteristics directly determine the activities required — breed-specific grooming, patient-specific procedures, item-specific repair.
Subject and participants are related — participants commission, fund, or authorise services on or for the subject — but they are independently defined.
Different customer segments may involve different subject types, but the segment is defined by its needs and willingness to pay, not by the subject.

userFacing.shortDescription: An entity involved in a service engagement in a defined role — customer, payer, commissioner, decision-maker, or any other role.

purposiveDescription.description: Any person or organisation involved in a service engagement in a defined role. The person who pays, the organisation that commissions, the carer who makes decisions, the expert called in for assessment — any entity with influence on how the service proceeds. When you identify your service participants, the system tracks who is involved, in what capacity, and how their status affects the service workflow. The set of possible roles is open — the model does not constrain what kinds of participation your service may involve.

weightedRelationships.rationale: The participant's role is defined in relation to the subject — they commission, fund, authorise, or contribute to the service on or for the subject.
The participant influences the offering — a commissioner may constrain scope, a payer may limit options — but the offering is primarily shaped by the subject's needs.
Participants often belong to or represent a customer segment, but the mapping is characterising — a segment is not defined by its participants.
Governance requirements may apply to participants (commissioner must approve, payer must authorise), but the primary governance binding is to the subject.

name: ActivityType
doc:
A defined type of activity within the business.
Every activity has a type, and every type belongs
to one of the five taxonomy categories.

userFacing.shortDescription: A defined kind of business activity, classified into one of five categories.

purposiveDescription.description: Something your business does — an identifiable unit of work that the system holds, tracks, and uses. In this system, every activity is an activity of one of the following types: service delivery, enabling, governance, development, or overhead. When you assign one of these types to an activity, the system will use that information to plan resources, allocate costs, and verify that governance requirements are being met for each kind of work.

weightedRelationships.rationale: Cost allocation is structurally determined by activity type — every cost line traces back to an activity category.
Granularity level directly governs how an activity type is tracked and costed — envelope vs category vs tracked.
Budgets aggregate by activity type but the relationship is indirect — mediated through cost allocation.
Activity records are typed by activity type but the record is an operational artefact, not a structural dependency.
Resources are consumed by activities but the mapping is many-to-many and context-dependent.
Channels deliver services which contain activities, but the relationship is distant — mediated through service offerings.

doc:

userFacing.shortDescription: A recorded instance of an activity that actually happened.

name: ActivityGranularity
doc:
Policy declaration: the granularity level at which
activity is tracked for a given business area.

userFacing.shortDescription: A policy declaration of how precisely activity is tracked in a given area.

purposiveDescription.description: A policy declaration: how precisely does your business track activity in a given area? The system supports three levels — envelope (a rough total), category (broken down by type), and tracked (every individual activity recorded). Different parts of your business can operate at different levels at the same time, and you can refine the level as your needs evolve.

weightedRelationships.rationale: Granularity governs how activity types are tracked. If the granularity policy changes, the activity types in that area may need reviewing — but a policy change about tracking precision does not redefine what the activity type is.

name: ActivityCostAllocation
doc:
The mapping from an activity (or aggregate) to its
financial cost. Makes resource consumption visible
to the financial model.

userFacing.shortDescription: The mapping from an activity type to its financial cost.

purposiveDescription.description: The mapping from an activity to its financial cost — how much does it cost each time this kind of work is done? When you define cost allocations, the system can connect your activity model to your financial model, making resource consumption visible in financial terms.

weightedRelationships.rationale: Cost allocations are defined per activity type. If the allocation changes (method, estimated cost), the activity type may need reviewing — but a financial change to how the activity is costed does not redefine what the activity type is.

Cost allocations use cost driver rates to compute per-activity costs. If the allocation method changes, the cost driver may need reviewing — but the driver describes the resource's cost behaviour independently of how individual activities are costed against it.
Cost allocations ultimately feed unit economics through cost drivers. If an allocation changes, unit economics may need updating — but the relationship is mediated through cost drivers, not direct.

doc:

userFacing.shortDescription: A category of resource needed to run the service — people, equipment, premises, or external services.

purposiveDescription.description: A kind of thing your business needs in order to operate — staff, equipment, premises, technology, or external services such as a laboratory or a contractor. The system holds each resource type as a tracked concept. When you define your resource types, the system uses them to plan capacity, understand your cost base, and identify where you might be constrained.

weightedRelationships.rationale: Instances are typed by ResourceType. If the type definition changes (category, cost profile, capacity unit), every instance of that type needs reassessment.

Constraints are scoped to specific resource types. If the resource type changes, the constraints that limit its availability need reassessment — a constraint on a specific resource assumes specific properties of that type.

Capabilities combine resources into service functions. A change to a resource type may require reviewing the capabilities that use it, but capabilities are resilient to substitution within a resource category.

Capacity models describe throughput given a resource configuration. A change to a resource type may affect throughput calculations, but the relationship is mediated through the specific configuration.
Cost drivers are linked to resources. A change to a resource type (especially its cost profile) may require reviewing the associated cost driver, but the link is structural rather than definitional.
Activities consume resources. A change to a resource type may affect which activities can be performed, but the coupling is many-to-many and context-dependent.

name: RegisteredTemplate
doc:
An Operational Template (OPT) registered in the CDR.
Templates compose archetypes into use-case-specific
data sets. Each template defines one composition type.
Uploaded via the Definition API (POST /definition/template/adl1.4).
EHRbase rejects duplicate template_id uploads (HTTP 409).

name: Composition
doc:
A composition committed to the CDR.
Compositions are the unit of clinical data committed
and retrieved. Each conforms to a registered template.
Canonical JSON format maps directly to the openEHR
Reference Model hierarchy:
  COMPOSITION > content > ENTRY > data/description > items
Commit returns 204

name: AqlQuery
doc:
A named AQL (Archetype Query Language) query.
AQL queries the CDR by archetype type, providing
entity views independent of the process that produced
the data. Paths mirror the RM hierarchy using archetype
node IDs (at-codes).
